overview:
Kankali Tila, often called the Jaini Mound, is one of the most important archaeological sites for reconstructing the early history of Jainism in North India. Located to the southwest of present-day Mathura in Uttar Pradesh, India, the mound is roughly rectangular in shape, measuring about 500 feet in length and 350 feet in breadth. Its modern name derives from a small temple dedicated to the Hindu goddess Kankali (a form of Durga) situated nearby, but the archaeological record reveals that this area was, for many centuries, a major Jain religious and artistic center.

Systematic excavations at Kankali Tila were carried out between 1871 and 1896, with key seasons in 1888–1891 under figures such as Alexander Cunningham, Alois Anton Führer, and James Burgess. These excavations uncovered the remains of at least two Jain temples (one associated with the Digambara community and one with the Śvetāmbara community), a Jain stupa, extensive architectural fragments (pillars, railings, gateways, crossbeams, lintels), and a large corpus of sculptures and inscribed votive tablets known as ayagapattas (tablets of homage). The discoveries were crucial in demonstrating, on archaeological grounds, that Jains built stupas and large temple complexes, something that had previously been known primarily from textual sources.

The material from Kankali Tila spans a remarkably long chronological range. Inscriptions found at the site date from around the 2nd century BCE to the 11th–12th century CE, indicating continuous or recurrent Jain occupation and patronage for at least twelve centuries. Many of the sculptures belong to the Kushan period (roughly 1st–4th century CE), when Mathura served as a major urban and political center and, at times, as a southern capital of the Kushan Empire. The site has yielded numerous images of Jain Tirthankaras—such as Ṛṣabhanātha, Neminātha, Pārśvanātha, and Mahāvīra—along with guardian deities and richly decorated ayagapattas bearing auspicious symbols (dharmacakra, elephants, fish, kalasha, etc.) and dedicatory inscriptions.

The inscriptions from Kankali Tila provide valuable insight into the social composition and organization of the Jain community in ancient Mathura. Donors include merchants, artisans, perfumers, dyers, ironmongers, courtesans, and members of various professional groups, reflecting the strong connection between Jainism and urban mercantile networks. The repeated mention of donations for railings, tablets, and images suggests a vibrant culture of lay patronage and temple-based worship. These records also help establish a relative chronology for the development of Jain art and epigraphy, with references to rulers such as the Northern Satrap Sodāsa and the Kushan emperor Kaniṣka, as well as dates expressed in regnal years.

Art historically, Kankali Tila is recognized as one of the largest centers of Jain sculpture. Excavations between 1888 and 1891 alone yielded over 700 artifacts, including Tirthankara images, sculptures of attendant deities, and ayagapattas. Many of these objects are now housed in the State Jain Museum at Mathura, where they are displayed alongside plaster casts and Jain miniature paintings. The site has thus become a key reference point for understanding the evolution of Jain iconography—from relatively simple early representations to more elaborate, multi-figure compositions—and for tracing stylistic connections between Mathura and other regions.

From the perspective of Jain religious history, Kankali Tila demonstrates that Mathura was not only a major Hindu pilgrimage center associated with Krishna, but also a long-standing Jain hub. The continuous sequence of inscriptions and images shows that Jain communities flourished here under different political regimes, including the Indo-Scythians, Kushans, Guptas, and later medieval powers. The presence of both Digambara and Śvetāmbara remains at the same mound highlights the complex sectarian landscape and suggests overlapping or successive phases of occupation rather than a simple, exclusive claim by one tradition. As a result, Kankali Tila is frequently cited in modern scholarship and community education as a foundational site for the study of Jain archaeology, art, and social history.

Today, while the mound itself is largely an archaeological zone, its legacy continues through museum collections, academic research, and Jain community memory. Kankali Tila stands as a material testimony to the depth and continuity of Jain presence in the Mathura region, offering a rare, stratified record of religious architecture, devotional practice, and artistic production over more than a millennium.

primary_sources.title: Ayagapata of Pārśvanātha from Kankali Tila
primary_sources.author: Anonymous donor (inscriptional record)
primary_sources.translation: “Homage to the Arhats …” (followed by the name of the donor and details of the dedication of this tablet in the Jain temple).
primary_sources.notes: This ayagapata (tablet of homage) from Kankali Tila, dated roughly to the 1st century CE, bears an image of a Jina (identified with Pārśvanātha) surrounded by auspicious symbols such as a dharmacakra, elephants, fish, and a kalasha. The inscription begins with the standard Jain formula of reverence to the Arhats and then records the name of the donor—often a layperson connected to mercantile or artisanal professions—and the act of establishing the tablet in a Jain shrine. The language is early Prakrit, written in a regional Brahmi script, and the text is an important witness to early Jain devotional epigraphy in Mathura.

primary_sources.title: Ayagapata Inscription of Sodāsa (Northern Satrap)
primary_sources.author: Anonymous donor under the reign of Sodāsa
primary_sources.original_text: 𑀫𑀸𑀣𑀼𑀭𑀸𑀲𑀸 𑀲𑁄𑀤𑀸𑀲𑀸 𑀯𑀺𑀭𑀸𑀓𑀺 𑀓𑀺𑀦𑀺 𑀲𑀸𑀢𑀸𑀭𑀺𑀓𑀺 𑀓𑀺𑀦𑀺 𑀓𑀺𑀭𑀺𑀓𑀺 ...
primary_sources.transliteration: māthurāsā sodāsasa virāgi kiṇi sātāriki kiṇi kiri kiṇi ...
primary_sources.translation: “In Mathura, in the year 42 of King Sodāsa, this (tablet/image) was caused to be made and established …” (paraphrased, with regnal year and donor details).
primary_sources.notes: One of the ayagapattas from Kankali Tila carries an inscription mentioning the year 42 of the reign of the Northern Satrap ruler Sodāsa, placing it in the early 1st century CE. The text records the commissioning of a votive tablet or image by a lay donor during Sodāsa’s rule in Mathura. This inscription is significant for correlating Jain devotional activity with the political chronology of the Northern Satraps and for confirming that Jain communities were active patrons of religious art under their administration.

primary_sources.title: Dhanamitra Ayagapata
primary_sources.author: Dhanamitra (named donor)
primary_sources.translation: “Homage to the Arhats. Dhanamitra has caused this (tablet) to be made …”
primary_sources.notes: The Dhanamitra ayagapata, dated to around 25 CE, is another important votive tablet from Kankali Tila. It features a central Jina image with surrounding symbols and an inscription naming Dhanamitra as the donor. The formula of homage to the Arhats followed by the donor’s name and the act of dedication reflects a standard pattern in Jain epigraphy at Mathura. This tablet contributes to our understanding of individual lay patrons and the continuity of Jain worship practices in the early Kushan period.

primary_sources.title: Kankali Tila Inscriptions of Kaniṣka (Years 5 and 7)
primary_sources.author: Anonymous donors under Emperor Kaniṣka
primary_sources.original_text: 𑀫𑀸𑀣𑀼𑀭𑀸 𑀓𑀺𑀦𑀺𑀱𑀓𑀸𑀲𑀺 𑀯𑀺𑀭𑀸𑀓𑀺 𑀤𑀸𑀣𑀺 𑀕𑀺𑀭𑀺 𑀕𑀺𑀭𑀺 ...
primary_sources.transliteration: māthurā kaniṣkasa virāgi dāthi giri giri ... (Year 5 / Year 7)
primary_sources.translation: “In Mathura, in the year 5 (or 7) of King Kaniṣka, this (object) was caused to be made …” (paraphrased, with regnal year and donor information).
primary_sources.notes: Several inscriptions from Kankali Tila refer to regnal years of the Kushan emperor Kaniṣka, notably years 5 and 7. These texts, associated with Jain votive objects, confirm that Jain communities continued to commission religious art and architecture under Kushan rule. The inscriptions help anchor the chronology of Jain sculpture at Mathura within the broader framework of Kushan imperial history and demonstrate the integration of Jain religious life into the political and economic milieu of the time.

misconceptions.myth: Kankali Tila is primarily a Hindu site associated only with the worship of the goddess Kankali and has little to do with Jainism.
misconceptions.reality: While the modern name of the mound comes from a small temple dedicated to the Hindu goddess Kankali, archaeological excavations have shown that Kankali Tila was historically one of the largest centers of Jain religious activity and sculpture in Mathura. The site has yielded Jain temples, a Jain stupa, hundreds of Tirthankara images, ayagapattas, and inscriptions spanning more than a millennium of Jain presence.

misconceptions.myth: Only one Jain sect (either Digambara or Śvetāmbara) was active at Kankali Tila, making it an exclusive sectarian site.
misconceptions.reality: Excavations have revealed remains of at least two Jain temples at Kankali Tila, one associated with the Digambara community and another with the Śvetāmbara community. This indicates that the mound was used by different Jain traditions over time and cannot be claimed exclusively by a single sect. The material record suggests a complex, overlapping sectarian history rather than a simple, uniform affiliation.

misconceptions.myth: Jains did not build stupas; the stupa form is exclusively Buddhist, and any mound at Mathura must therefore be Buddhist in origin.
misconceptions.reality: The excavations at Kankali Tila provided clear archaeological evidence of a Jain stupa, confirming that Jains also adopted and adapted the stupa form for their own religious purposes. Prior to these discoveries, the existence of Jain stupas was known mainly from textual references. Kankali Tila thus plays a crucial role in demonstrating that stupa architecture was part of Jain as well as Buddhist religious practice.

misconceptions.myth: The Jain presence in Mathura was brief and marginal, overshadowed entirely by other religious communities.
misconceptions.reality: Inscriptions from Kankali Tila range from the 2nd century BCE to the 11th–12th century CE, showing that Jain communities were active in Mathura for at least twelve centuries. The large number of sculptures, votive tablets, and donor records indicates a sustained and significant Jain presence, closely tied to the city’s mercantile and artisanal classes. Mathura was simultaneously a major center for multiple religious traditions, including Jainism.
